Main talk · 1 of 22

MARES: Magnetic Remnants in Symbiotics

Open with the number, then give the audience the question.

In my own words

What would tell us that a white dwarf is magnetic when the brightest thing we see in the optical is the red giant beside it? In CH Cygni, our clue was a pulse in X-rays. The source brightens and fades every eleven minutes and twenty-two seconds. I’m Manuel Pichardo Marcano. This is work with Tom Maccarone, Liliana Rivera Sandoval, and the MARES team. I’ll show you how we found that period and what we think is turning.

If I have more time

MARES stands for Magnetic Remnants in Symbiotics. CH Cyg is the first result I’ll show. Then I’ll come back to what we can do across the population.

Main talk · 2 of 22

Symbiotic Stars

Point to the giant first and follow the gas toward its companion.

In my own words

Follow the stream in the illustration from the donor on the left to the disc on the right. The artist drew a pulsar binary. In the symbiotics we study, the donor is a red giant and the compact companion is usually a white dwarf. It can capture some of the wind the giant sheds. In a close enough system the giant can also transfer gas through its Roche lobe. Their orbit can take hundreds of days or even years. The eleven-minute clock I just mentioned is already telling us about a much smaller part of this picture. In our catalogue snapshot there are 284 confirmed systems in the Milky Way. Even that sample took decades to assemble.

If I have more time

The 751 on the slide adds together suspected, possible, and likely systems. For scale, one population model predicts about 53,000 in the Galaxy. The model and the catalogue are answering different questions.

Passages to practice with

Check when rehearsing

The local catalogue gives 284 confirmed Milky Way systems and 751 other entries (627 suspected, 78 possible, 46 likely). Laversveiler & Gonçalves report 800–4,100 as an empirical lower-limit range and (53 ± 6) × 10³ as a model prediction. The artwork shows a pulsar binary and illustrates the gas flow.

Main talk · 3 of 22

Why Magnetism?

Trace the formation diagram from left to right.

In my own words

Start with the example on the right, FN Sagittarii. In the model by Belloni and colleagues, a common-envelope episode leaves a white dwarf. It has time to cool and start crystallizing before its companion becomes a giant. Later the wind brings in angular momentum and spins the white dwarf up. The authors propose that rotation and crystallization together can amplify its magnetic field. Now follow one parcel of gas arriving today. If the field is strong enough, it can lift gas out of the inner disc and guide it toward a magnetic pole. That last step gives us something to observe.

If I have more time

The prediction about many magnetic white dwarfs applies to systems formed through that channel, with an old enough companion. FN Sgr is their worked example. The abundance in the wider population is the question for the survey.

Passages to practice with

Check when rehearsing

Belloni et al. explicitly condition the population prediction on their formation channel and a donor main-sequence lifetime of at least about 3 Gyr.

Main talk · 4 of 22

The Evidence So Far

Use Z And to explain why a signal can be easy to miss.

In my own words

Z And shows how much luck can go into finding one of these clocks. Sokoloski and Bildsten kept seeing a 28-minute oscillation over a year. As an outburst faded, the modulation fell from about five millimagnitudes to about two. The later survey of 35 symbiotics found one clear magnetic accretor, Z And itself. For 25 objects their upper limits went from roughly two to thirteen millimagnitudes. A Z And signal at its faintest could slip below every one of those limits. That changes how I read the shortest bar on this slide. Only a few percent have reported candidates. The underlying magnetic fraction is still open.

If I have more time

The bars provide context. The field white dwarfs, the nearby cataclysmic variables, and the symbiotics were selected and tested in different ways. The old proposal counted seven candidates. The deck rounds a broader list, including tentative cases, to about ten.

Passages to practice with

Check when rehearsing

The deck’s “about ten” includes tentative reports. One detection in a survey of 35 and a catalogue tally of roughly ten out of 284 have different selection functions. Neither yields an unbiased magnetic fraction.

Main talk · 5 of 22

The MARES Survey

Point to TESS, then XMM-Newton.

In my own words

We designed MARES around two questions. Where can we find repeating signals, and which of them trace accretion onto the white dwarf? TESS gives us long optical light curves in which we can look for weak periods and revisit known ones. Our Cycle 7 proposal targeted 110 confirmed symbiotic binaries. In X-rays the red giant contributes much less to the light we’re timing, so we get a clearer view of the accreting star. For CH Cyg we could start immediately with an observation already in the XMM-Newton archive.

If I have more time

The proposal asked for fast sampling to resolve minute-scale variability. Its analysis plan specifies 20 seconds and its example target table lists 120 seconds. I describe the 110 as the proposed sample. Any count of delivered short-cadence light curves needs its own accounting.

Passages to practice with

Check when rehearsing

The proposal establishes the requested target list. Its prose requests 20 s, while the sample table lists 120 s. An awarded cadence or count of observed targets needs an observing record.

Main talk · 6 of 22

CH Cygni

Give the old period and the new question room to land.

In my own words

Here is why we went back to CH Cyg. It is nearby, it changes brightness dramatically, and Chandra has actually imaged its jet. In 1990 a group reported an optical oscillation at roughly 500 seconds and associated it with a rotating magnetic white dwarf. Follow-up teams looked in the same period range and came away empty-handed. An earlier X-ray search also found variability without a convincing clock. Decades later, the basic question was still a good one. Could we see a repeatable pulse from the accreting white dwarf itself?

If I have more time

The jet is a reason to ask about magnetism. The pulse is the measurement we use to address it. Keep the two numbers distinct as we move on. The historical optical claim was around 500 seconds. Our X-ray measurement is around 682.

Passages to practice with

Check when rehearsing

Main talk · 7 of 22

Searching for a Period

Run a finger along the trial-period axis and stop at the narrow peak.

In my own words

On 24 May 2018, XMM-Newton observed CH Cyg in a high state. The pn camera gave us just over 34 kiloseconds, about nine and a half hours, at nearly four counts per second. Imagine choosing a trial period and cutting the observation into pieces of that length. Stack those pieces and see whether the same phases keep coming out bright. We repeated that for 300 trial periods. Along the bottom is the period we tried. Up the side is how poorly a constant count rate fits the folded profile. See that isolated peak? That is where the cycles line up best. Now let’s look at what we stacked.

If I have more time

The search was done with pn because it collected the most photons. We then folded MOS1 and MOS2 at the pn period. Those are checks with separate cameras during the same observation.

Passages to practice with

Check when rehearsing

The pn rate is 3.76 counts/s. The 34.3 ks exposure is 9.53 hours. The high-state identification comes from the paper’s discussion of the 2018 observation.

Main talk · 8 of 22

A 682.5 s X-ray Period

Pause at the top of the first hump. Trace one cycle before pointing to the second.

In my own words

Now the horizontal axis is phase. From zero to one you see the count rate rise, fall, and begin to rise again. From one to two we’ve drawn the same cycle a second time so you can follow the shape across the edge. The period is 682.5 seconds, with an uncertainty of seven seconds. The fractional rms amplitude is about four percent. Even a modulation that small can emerge when you line up this many cycles. We also recover it when we fold each MOS light curve at the pn period. The main peak is clear. There is a hint of a second one, and I’d want more data before building a two-pole picture around it.

If I have more time

If someone is comparing the numbers on the slide, we used eight phase bins for the search statistic, giving seven degrees of freedom and chi-square of 103. The paper reports a trials-adjusted false-alarm probability of order ten to the minus seventeen under that test. The displayed profile uses 32 bins to show the shape.

Passages to practice with

Check when rehearsing

Table 1 lists 0.04 fractional rms. The ±7 s comes from a Gaussian fit to the width of the folding peak. The false-alarm probability is the paper’s value under its stated trial-period test.

Main talk · 9 of 22

A Magnetic White Dwarf

Point first to the pole, then to each field estimate.

In my own words

Our interpretation is that the white dwarf is rotating. Gas follows field lines toward a small region near a magnetic pole. As that region turns with the star, the X-ray flux we see changes with spin phase. That lets us ask how strong the field would have to be. First, to guide the gas before it reaches the surface requires a field of order ten thousand gauss or more for our adopted parameters. Second, if the star has reached spin equilibrium, we get a characteristic field of about a million gauss. The distinction between those two estimates matters. The second depends on the equilibrium assumption.

If I have more time

For the parameters in the paper, the estimated time to spin up is about twenty thousand years. That fits within the red giant’s mass-transfer phase and makes equilibrium plausible. A direct field measurement would be a different experiment.

Passages to practice with

Check when rehearsing

At the paper’s fiducial mass, radius and accretion rate, the channeling condition gives B ≳ 10⁴ G. Spin equilibrium gives B ≈ 10⁶ G. The corresponding spin-up timescale is 2 × 10⁴ yr. A measured upper bound on B would require another constraint.

Field estimates and spin-up · lines 196–238

Main talk · 10 of 22

Support for the Propeller Model

Describe what changes when the gas supply falls.

In my own words

The propeller idea makes a prediction we can try to test. When the gas supply is high, matter can push far enough in to reach the magnetic poles. When the supply drops, the magnetosphere can extend beyond the radius where gas orbits at the stellar spin rate. The rotating field can then give angular momentum to the inflow and expel material. A disc-instability picture has also been proposed for the state changes. Finding a spin signal establishes a piece of the propeller picture, a rotating magnetic accretor. What I’d like next is to follow CH Cyg through a change of state and see what happens to the pulse.

If I have more time

We can measure its amplitude and shape in each state and quote a sensitivity when it disappears from view. A faint observation on its own would leave open whether the pulse weakened or we simply ran out of photons.

Passages to practice with

Check when rehearsing

A rotating magnetic accretor supports the propeller interpretation. The test proposed in the paper is monitoring through high and quiescent states. Ejection by the propeller was not measured in this timing observation.

Model and test · lines 287–292 and 307–315

Main talk · 11 of 22

Do Hard X-rays Mean Magnetic?

Compare the two upper limits with the four-percent pulse you just showed.

In my own words

Hard X-rays tell us that some of the accreting gas gets very hot. Can we use that alone to pick magnetic systems? Consider RT Cru. It is bright in hard X-rays, yet our best observation gives an upper limit of about one percent rms. A pulse as strong as the four-percent pulse in CH Cyg would have stood out there. MWC 560 also has a jet, but we collected far fewer photons. Its limit is about twenty percent. A CH Cyg-like pulse could easily hide in those data. Both searches came back without a detection, and they teach us quite different things.

If I have more time

Hot gas in a boundary layer offers another way to make hard emission. V648 Car is an example discussed by Freitas and colleagues. Magnetic cataclysmic variables are useful analogues, but hard X-ray emission alone gives us no unique field diagnosis.

Passages to practice with

Check when rehearsing

Main talk · 12 of 22

Next: Spin Evolution in Z And

Point to the two periods and let the audience hear the difference.

In my own words

Z And gives us a different use for a clock. In 1997 and 1998 the optical period was 1,682.6 seconds. In TESS Sector 57, Merc and colleagues measured 1,601.9 seconds. Our analysis of that sector recovers essentially the same peak. The difference is about 81 seconds in roughly 25 years. If both periods trace the spin, we can see the white dwarf speeding up on a human timescale. Accreting matter carries angular momentum, so the natural next question is whether the torque is large enough to explain what we see.

If I have more time

The average difference works out to about three seconds per year. We have measurements separated by years. The rate could have changed in between, particularly during Z And’s long active phase. Our Sector 57 plot and the published TESS result also use the same epoch.

Passages to practice with

Check when rehearsing

Arithmetic from the two published optical periods gives 1,682.6 − 1,601.9 = 80.7 s, or about −3.2 s/yr averaged over 25 years. A continuous spin derivative has not been measured by these two epochs.

Two epochs · line 451

Main talk · 13 of 22

BF Cyg: Change in Waveform

Show the PDM dip, then the folded curve. Say “preliminary” before the number.

In my own words

BF Cyg gives us a warning about reading too much into the shape of a pulse. In the published B-band data the 1.806-hour signal had two humps in 2003 and one in 2004. The surviving hump lined up with one of the earlier ones. That is why the authors suggested a change in which accreting pole was visible or active. On this slide we show something preliminary from TESS. In Sector 14 we folded the light curve at 89.9 minutes and got a three-hump profile. That period is almost exactly three of the thirty-minute sampling intervals. I’d like to see it recur at faster cadence before attaching a spin interpretation to it.

If I have more time

The 108-minute published result and the 89.9-minute feature belong to different data sets. Checking the sampling and comparing the later 200-second full-frame data would help distinguish an alias, a transient disc oscillation, and a persistent stellar signal.

Passages to practice with

Check when rehearsing

89.9/30 ≈ 3 samples per cycle. That arithmetic flags a sampling check. It does not establish an alias. The BF Cyg passage is active in Misc/New.tex and commented out in the main proposal. Merc et al.’s target table lists Sectors 74 and 81 in parentheses as planned at the time of writing.

Main talk · 14 of 22

More Science with the Same Data

Walk the audience through the RT Cru traces before giving the population number.

In my own words

We can do more with the same light curves even when there’s no stable period. Look at RT Cru. One stretch is relatively quiet. In later TESS sectors the rapid, irregular fluctuations are obvious. This is flickering, and it tells us about the changing accretion flow. In their TESS study, Merc and colleagues identified 20 symbiotics with flickering-like variability, including 13 new examples. Among a selected group of accreting-only systems, 22 out of 27 showed flickering. That denominator matters because these are the systems in which it is easiest to see the disc.

If I have more time

An outburst gives us a related opportunity. In Z And the optical pulse changed amplitude as the outburst faded. Catching an event lets us follow the slow change in brightness and the fast variability in the very same light curve.

Passages to practice with

Check when rehearsing

The 22/27 subset comprises accreting-only symbiotics with previous flickering detections or usable TESS data. The RT Cru traces show different observations on different dates.

Main talk · 15 of 22

Next Steps

Give the optical and X-ray observing plans one sentence each, then explain the decision.

In my own words

On the optical side, I want to find new candidates and return to known systems to see whether the same periods come back. When a peak turns up, the first questions are whether it belongs to the target, whether the sampling can produce it, and whether it persists in a different sector. On the X-ray side, CH Cyg gives us a specific period to follow across accretion states. We can ask whether the pulse gets weaker, whether its shape changes, and eventually whether its period drifts. Putting the two bands together is how we get from a list of interesting periods to a physical picture.

If I have more time

For the survey, an observation with no pulse still contributes if we know what amplitude we could have detected. I’d like to carry that sensitivity information into any estimate of how common magnetism is.

Main talk · 16 of 22

Summary

Finish on the measurement and the next observable. Leave a beat for questions.

In my own words

If you remember one number, it’s 682.5 seconds. That’s how often the X-ray pulse repeated in our CH Cyg observation. We interpret it as the spin of a magnetic white dwarf. CH Cyg joins R Aquarii as the second white-dwarf symbiotic with detected X-ray pulsations, and both have jets. Now we have a clock to follow when CH Cyg changes state. Does it keep ticking where we can see it? That is the observation I would most like to show you next. Thank you.

If I have more time

The wider MARES question is how many other apparently quiet symbiotics hide similar clocks, and which of our observations are sensitive enough to find them.

Candidate Spin Periods

Which other systems have a candidate clock?

In my own words

I’d separate these examples by what was measured. In Z And we can follow an optical period across epochs. In R Aquarii the published X-ray modulation is 1,734 seconds. For CH Cyg the old 500-second optical claim and our 682.5-second X-ray measurement are separate entries in the history of one system. In the TESS sample, AE Cir has a 27.3-minute feature and CI Cyg a 66.6-minute candidate. The association with the target on the sky is less secure for CI Cyg. That is one reason I use the word “candidate” for this table.

If I have more time

The local catalogue even puts question marks beside some of its spin entries, including T CrB and SS73 122. The evidence for individual rows is worth more than a single total.

Power Spectrum

Can you see it with a different timing method?

In my own words

Yes. This is a Fourier power spectrum of the same XMM-Newton light curve. The red dashed line marks the frequency corresponding to 682.5 seconds, about 1.47 millihertz. You can see power there on top of a variable continuum. The search slide stacked cycles in phase. Here we are looking at power by frequency. Their agreement is a cross-check on the analysis of this observation. A second observation would answer the separate question about persistence.

If I have more time

We used POWSPEC with Leahy normalization for this figure. The quoted search significance comes from the epoch-folding statistic on slide 8.

CH Cyg with ASCA in 1994

Did ASCA see the same pulse in 1994?

In my own words

We went back to the ASCA data and ran the folding search. It gave no significant period. When we fold at the known XMM period, the plotted count rate varies at roughly the one-to-two-percent level. That is interesting to look at, but we treat the ASCA observation as a nondetection. Its count rate was about half a count per second, compared with 3.8 in pn. The reported fluxes were of similar order and were measured in different energy bands. Both sensitivity and a change in the pulse itself remain plausible.

If I have more time

The paper’s estimated ASCA sensitivity is about three percent rms under the adopted threshold. The one-to-two-percent figure describes the variation seen in a forced fold. Those quantities answer different questions.

Passages to practice with

Check when rehearsing

The reported fluxes were 6.9 × 10⁻¹¹ erg cm⁻² s⁻¹ for ASCA (2–10 keV) and 7.5 × 10⁻¹¹ for XMM-Newton (0.2–10 keV). A forced fold at a known period does not establish a detection.

Detecting a Pulsation

How strong would a pulse have to be for each observation?

In my own words

Pick one row. RT Cru in 2023 had about 0.8 counts per second for 59 kiloseconds. Under the assumptions in the table, we could have seen a coherent pulse of roughly one percent rms. Now look at MWC 560. The count rate is a hundred times lower and the limit is about twenty percent. To estimate these limits we assumed a narrow signal, a frequency width of one over the exposure, and a variability signal-to-noise threshold of five. Those assumptions are what allow us to compare the observations on the same footing.

If I have more time

For a narrow signal the expression on screen simplifies to one half times the total counts times the squared fractional rms. At a fixed threshold it takes roughly four times as many counts to reach half the pulse amplitude. This is a sensitivity estimate. Our CH Cyg discovery statistic was the epoch-folding chi-square.

Passages to practice with

Check when rehearsing

For λ = 1/T the expression reduces to SNRᵥₐᵣ = ½ I T r², with T in seconds for I in counts/s. The upper limits in Table 1 assume SNRᵥₐᵣ = 5. Their convention differs from the epoch-folding chi-square.

Backup · 22 of 22

TESS and Symbiotics

What can TESS actually measure in these giants?

In my own words

The comparison population is the point of this diagram. Merc and colleagues processed 335 apparently single red giants alongside the symbiotics. At a given brightness, a symbiotic with excess rapid variability stands out against that reference population. Then you inspect the light curve, the power spectrum, and the aperture to see whether flickering from the target makes sense. A TESS pixel is 21 arcseconds across, so a neighbour can contribute light. At the opposite extreme, CH Cyg saturated in their extraction. That is a practical reason to combine an optical survey with X-ray timing.

If I have more time

The quoted fraction near eighty percent belongs to the selected accreting-only sample with prior detections or usable light curves. The 20 TESS detections and 13 new flickering sources refer to the broader search.

Passages to practice with

Check when rehearsing

The saturation statement applies to the TESS flickering extraction analysed by Merc et al. in CH Cyg. In this talk the CH Cyg pulse is measured with XMM-Newton.
